analysis.one_liner: Bans mid-decade congressional redistricting and requires states to draw House maps with independent commissions.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban mid-decade congressional redistricting and require independent map-drawing commissions was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on September 17, 2025, with no cosponsors, and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop states from redrawing congressional district maps more than once every ten years, ending the practice of parties remapping districts mid-cycle to gain seats. It would also require every state to hand map-drawing to an independent commission made up of citizens who cannot have recently held office or worked in politics, with public meetings, an open website where anyone can submit their own map, and strict rules against considering voters' party affiliation or where incumbents live. If a legislature rejects the commission's plan, courts would pick or draw the map instead, and states would receive federal money to run their commissions.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters in states where legislators currently draw their own district lines: their House elections would become more competitive and their votes would count more evenly, because map-drawers could no longer consider party affiliation, voting history, or incumbents' addresses. Voters in states whose legislatures remap districts mid-decade to lock in a partisan advantage would be protected from having their districts redrawn between censuses.

how_it_helps.text: Bars a state from redrawing its congressional map more than once per decade, except when a court orders a new map to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act — eliminating mid-cycle gerrymanders.

Requires each state to draw its congressional districts through an independent commission whose members cannot have held office, run for office, or worked for a party or candidate in the previous four years, and bars the commission from considering voters' party affiliation or where incumbent House members live.

Requires public commission meetings, a public website with interactive mapping tools anyone can use to submit their own plan, and public hearings around the state before a plan is sent to the legislature.

Sets neutral criteria — equal population, Voting Rights Act compliance, keeping counties and municipalities together, compact and contiguous districts — and authorizes federal payments of $150,000 per House seat to help states run their commissions.

analysis.who_pays: State legislatures and incumbent members of Congress lose their ability to draw districts that favor their own party or protect incumbents. The federal government would pay states $150,000 per House seat to fund the commissions. Neither cost falls directly on taxpayers in a large way, but legislatures give up significant power.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans drawing districts based on voting history or party affiliation, which can make districts less geographically natural or split communities that vote alike, in pursuit of mathematical neutrality.
If a state's legislature rejects the commission's plan, the map is handed to the state's highest court or a federal district court, shifting line-drawing power to judges rather than voters.

The prohibition on mid-decade redistricting is written as a federal rule, raising the same federalism objection opponents have raised to past national redistricting standards: that the Constitution traditionally leaves districting to the states.
The ban applies only prospectively (redistricting after the 2030 census), so it would do nothing about maps already drawn today.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — permanently competitive, un-gerrymandered House elections — would be large, and the main costs are real but manageable: districts that ignore voting patterns can sometimes split communities of interest, and a nonpartisan commission drawn to neutral rules can still produce uncompetitive maps in a geographically sorted state. On balance the design is a serious, detailed attempt at the problem, but its enforceability against resistant states is its weakest point.

outcome.mechanism: A single member introduced the bill with no cosponsors; the House Judiciary Committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 17, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee, whose action history shows nothing further.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill's effective date was the redistricting cycle after the 2030 census, so it offered no change to maps in use today even if it had passed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Whoever benefits from the current system of legislator-drawn, mid-decade-remappable districts — incumbent officeholders and party mapmakers on both sides.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: With no cosponsors and no votes on record, the partisan shape of support and opposition was never tested; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities
industries.note: The bill takes map-drawing power away from legislators and their operatives, banning commissions from considering incumbent residences or partisan voting patterns, and locking maps in for the decade. Incumbents lose a tool for securing their seats.

industries.industry: Political consulting and redistricting software firms
industries.note: Gerrymandering is a lucrative, specialized industry; independent commissions with public mapping tools would shrink the market for partisan map-drawing services.

analysis.trajectory: A redistricting-reform bill with zero cosponsors and no committee action has effectively no path forward in this Congress; comparable measures have repeatedly stalled in committee, and the bill would not take effect until after the 2030 census even if enacted.
